title: Logging: what to record, at what level, and what it costs

videos.script: The server log is where you look first when something goes wrong. {{log}} It is also the one thing that was set up for you and never questioned. On Ubuntu it is a single file under slash var slash log, written by the server and cut every week by logrotate. {{file}} Out of the box it records very little: the server starting, the server stopping, errors, and checkpoints. A query that took ten seconds leaves no trace. Neither does a session that waited a minute for a lock. {{empty}} This lesson turns those on, one parameter at a time, and reads the lines each one writes. A slow statement. A lock wait, with the process that held the lock. A sort that spilled to disk. A connection arriving. {{lines}} Then it measures the price. Logging every statement sounds like the safe choice. On a fixed benchmark run it wrote almost nine megabytes, for ten thousand small transactions. {{bytes}} The rest is reading: finding the errors in a large file, knowing when rotation happens, and switching to JSON when a machine, not a person, is going to read the log. {{json}}
